title: Arion · lines 16–23
subtitle: In full costume, Arion sings his last song from the stern and leaps into the sea; a dolphin, so the story goes, carries him to Taenarum

notes.label: νόμος
notes.body: Here νόμος means a musical "strain" or set piece for solo singer and cithara, not "law". The ὄρθιος νόμος was a piece pitched high and clear.

notes.label: The dolphin
notes.body: Dolphins were associated with Apollo, patron of music, so a Greek audience would readily see divine help in the rescue of a great musician.

notes.label: Taenarum
notes.body: The southernmost point of mainland Greece (modern Cape Matapan), at the tip of the middle prong of the Peloponnese, with a sanctuary of Poseidon. Corinth lay far to the north.

notes.label: Irony
notes.body: The would-be murderers are filled with pleasure at the thought of a concert. Their delight in his music sits uneasily beside their plan to kill him.

notes.label: Superlative
notes.trans: the best singer in the world
notes.body: "The best singer of all mankind": even the crew recognise Arion's greatness, which makes their plan all the more shocking.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.quote: ἀνεχώρησαν ἐκ τῆς πρύμνης εἰς μέσην ναῦν
notes.trans: they withdrew from the stern amidships
notes.body: The crew move away from the stern, leaving it clear like a stage with its audience in front. The reader can picture the scene.

notes.label: Contrast
notes.body: The narrative switches from the crew (οἱ δέ) to Arion (ὁ δέ), setting the eager audience against the lone performer.

notes.label: Tricolon
notes.body: Three participles show Arion's preparation step by step: dressing, taking his cithara, taking his place. The reader sees his calm professionalism.

notes.label: Emphasis
notes.body: "All his finery": Arion leaves nothing out, which stresses his dignity and his pride in his art.

notes.label: Word choice
notes.body: The compound verb means he went right through the song from start to finish. He does not cut his performance short, even with death waiting.

notes.label: Tense
notes.body: The present participle means "as the song was ending": he leaps while the last notes are still sounding, with no pause at all.

notes.label: Vivid detail
notes.body: ἔρριψεν is a violent verb, "hurled", and it comes before its object. The leap is sudden and dramatic.

notes.label: Foreshadowing
notes.quote: ὡς εἶχε σὺν τῇ σκευῇ πάσῃ
notes.trans: just as he was, costume and all
notes.body: Arion jumps still wearing his costume. This detail will prove his story when he reappears in it in line 31.

notes.label: Polyptoton
notes.quote: πᾶσαν τὴν σκευὴν … τῇ σκευῇ πάσῃ
notes.trans: all his finery … all his finery
notes.body: The phrase returns in a different case and in reverse order, so the costume frames the whole performance from start to finish.

notes.label: Contrast (μέν ... δέ)
notes.body: The crew sail calmly on to Corinth while Arion's fate takes a miraculous turn. The balanced construction sets the two outcomes side by side.

notes.label: Emphatic position
notes.body: The subject is held back until after Arion's name and then opens the line, so the rescuer arrives as a surprise.

notes.label: Narrator's aside
notes.body: Herodotus reports the miracle as something people say, without vouching for it himself. The reader is left to wonder how much to believe.

notes.label: Fast pace
notes.trans: took him up and carried him to Taenarum
notes.body: The rescue is told in a handful of words, a sudden change of speed after the long build-up to the song.

questions: Why do you think the sailors were happy to let Arion perform before he died?
How does Herodotus slow the narrative down in lines 18–21, and why at this point?
What is the effect of ὡς λέγουσι in line 23? Does it make the story more or less believable?

context.body:
Arion came from Methymna, on the island of Lesbos, and was remembered as the greatest citharode (a singer who accompanied himself on the cithara) of the seventh century BC. Herodotus, who tells his story just before this passage, says that he was the first person known to have composed a dithyramb, a choral song in honour of Dionysus, to have given it a name and to have produced it at Corinth. Later Greeks regarded him as the man who turned the dithyramb into an organised art form, one of the roots of Athenian drama.

His rescue by a dolphin became one of the best-known stories of the ancient world. Herodotus ends his account by mentioning a small bronze figure of a man on a dolphin, dedicated by Arion at Taenarum, and the tale was retold by later writers such as Plutarch and pictured in Roman mosaics.
